title: Winter and summer warming in the North America sector
caption:
North America sector, SSP5-8.5, 2081–2100: winter 8.75 °C; summer 7.66 °C; winter minus summer +1.09 °C.
Season means weight months by calendar days; sector means use cell areas. Historical lines are simulations. Solid = DJF; dashed = JJA.

title: Winter vs. summer warming rates, 2015–2100
caption:
Arctic SSP5-8.5 winter trend: 2.519 °C/decade; summer: 1.011; difference: +1.508.
Ordinary least-squares trends over the same 86 season-years, 2015–2100. No uncertainty interval or significance test is estimated.

title: Regional winter and summer warming, 2081–2100
caption:
Largest winter-minus-summer anomaly contrast among these regions under SSP5-8.5: Arctic, +13.61 °C.
Bars average 20 complete seasons, 2081–2100. Geographic sectors include land and ocean; Arctic overlaps parts of the other sectors.

title: Where is the winter warming anomaly larger than summer’s?
caption:
Northern Hemisphere grid-cell SSP5-8.5 seasonal anomaly contrast spans -11.62 to +28.40 °C in 2081–2100.
Red = larger winter anomaly; blue = larger summer anomaly. Each season uses its own historical baseline. This is not a trend-rate map.

title: Winter–summer anomaly contrast by latitude, 2081–2100
caption:
Arctic area-mean seasonal anomaly contrast: +10.16 °C under SSP2-4.5 and +13.61 °C under SSP5-8.5.
Curves are equal-width longitude means at each native latitude. Positive values indicate a larger winter warming anomaly, not necessarily a faster local trend.

title: The winter–summer warming gap across regions and decades
caption:
Arctic SSP5-8.5 winter-minus-summer anomaly contrast: +4.22 °C in 2021–2030; +13.81 °C in 2091–2100.
Each cell averages ten complete season-year pairs. A positive contrast measures unequal warming since baseline, not the literal loss of winter.
